subject: [PATCH v1 0/3] mm/readahead: avoid per-folio memcg reclaim

reviews.author: Jan Kara
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Jan Kara noted that the patch does not handle the case where a folio is already mapped in another memcg, which could lead to incorrect reclaim behavior and requested additional checks to ensure correct handling of such cases.

Jan Kara questioned whether the folios being faulted are actually used before they get reclaimed, suggesting that if not, it would be more efficient to stop reading them in the first place.
sentiment_signals: questioning the effectiveness of the patch
reviews.raw_body:
Hello Joanne!

On Fri 02-10-26 17:15:52, Joanne Koong wrote:

---

I cannot really comment on how much sense this makes from memcg POV (I'll
defer to people understanding that area better). When I'm reading your
problem description I'm wondering about one thing: Are the folios we are
faulting around really used in your workloads before they get reclaimed?
Because what I'd expect to happen in cases under heavy memory pressure is
that ra->mmap_miss would quickly grow over the limit (100) and we'd just
stop doing mmap readahead for the files. If the read-around pages aren't
getting used before being evicted, then the first natural thing would be to
actually stop reading them in the first place :) The mmap_miss logic is
actually rather dumb so I wouldn't be surprised if it doesn't work in your
case...

The experiments you have conducted below indicate that if you effectively
disable readahead you get more page faults & smaller IO requests (expected)
but for your realistic loads under memory pressure is that really an
overall performance loss?

								Honza

2026-10-05.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in Linux's readahead mechanism by avoiding per-folio memory cgroup (memcg) reclaim. When multiple tasks fault in the same cgroup, the frequent per-folio charges trigger reclaim, leading to livelocks and high CPU usage. The patches modify readahead to charge all folios in its window at once when the memcg is at its limit, reducing the number of reclaim passes by 94-96% and eliminating livelocks on a test system with btrfs file systems and compress-force=zstd:3.
